resolutions.rationale: The comparison supplies concrete dates and quantities, but its source equivalence and chronology remain sufficiently contested for medium confidence.
The named external witnesses are identifiable, but their independence and precise referential force are not fully demonstrated in the source.
Unattainable certainty is an improper standard, but denial analogies do not show that the opponent used that standard.
Holocaust and lunar-landing denials illustrate excessive doubt but provide no evidence about this historical record.
It addresses a possible skeptical method, though Carrier’s case is not accurately reduced to demanding certainty.
Burden standards matter, but the move cannot substitute for establishing which explanation best fits the evidence.
Comparing mythicism with Holocaust or lunar-landing denial materially weakens the representation of the live alternative.
The denial analogies and their limited connection to Carrier’s actual standard are explicit enough to support high assessment confidence.
Roswell, Ned Ludd, and cargo-cult examples are concrete, but their comparability to Christian origins requires unresolved inferential bridges.
Membership in a class of fictional deities can affect a prior, but the proposed class may be selected too broadly.
The common attributes are asserted broadly without enough named cases or controls for important differences.
The reference class directly supports Carrier’s proposed prior against assuming a uniquely historical savior deity.
A defensible comparison class would materially advance the nonexistence model, though it cannot decide the evidence alone.
Terms such as savior, passion, victory over death, and earthly story require sharper inclusion criteria.
Saying all members share the listed features and none existed overstates an incompletely demonstrated comparison.
The preexistent-angel model is recoverable from the source, but its identification with earliest Christian belief remains contestable.
Epistles, later gospels, and the proposed direction of development are plainly distinguished.
The categorical description of Paul and all later attestation leaves insufficient room for ambiguous or independent evidence.
The chronology is clear, but describing Paul as celestial and later gospels as crafted fiction bundles disputed interpretations.
The omission pattern coherently reduces expected earthly anchoring without making silence logically decisive.
Specific omissions, archons, interpolation, and vocabulary are cited, though several disputed readings are treated briskly.
The move squarely challenges the affirmative's earliest and most important documentary evidence.
Systematic absence of expected earthly anchors materially advances Pauline ambiguity.
The absent birth, killer, burial, and setting details are concrete and readily auditable.
The move identifies ambiguity but sometimes presents contested interpolation and demonic readings as more settled than shown.
The textual pattern is fairly described, but it underplays the possibility of both revelation and human transmission.
The categorical conclusion that criteria cannot recover history is stronger than the summarized methodological critique establishes.
The literary indicators are identifiable, but the inference from constructed narrative to wholesale historical unsuitability remains disputed.
The source expressly separates silence, fiction, and dependence claims, making the inference and its limitations assessable with high confidence.
The move offers a plausible alternative explanation without denying that Paul gives little biographical detail.
Showing material disanalogies coherently weakens the proposed reference class and derivation inference.
Named specialists, publications, and concrete Attis and Osiris differences support the challenge, though mostly by authority.
The reply directly targets the decisive claim that contemporary savior deities shared a genuine death-resurrection pattern.
Defeating the proposed comparative class materially protects the Jewish and historical explanation.
The reply distinguishes reanimation, bodily resurrection, and Jewish eschatological resurrection with useful specificity.
The reply reports rejection without reconstructing the strongest specific parallels Carrier actually offered.
Accurate research is not odd for historical fiction, so the asserted improbability does not follow without a base rate.
Archaeological use is asserted generally without showing Jesus-specific discoveries or comparing historically situated fiction.
The reply contacts Carrier’s literary-fiction claim by arguing that detailed historical fit needs explanation.
Authorial competence is relevant to gospel evaluation but does not itself demonstrate the protagonist’s existence.
The core challenge is understandable, though “real people, events, and perhaps places” combines separable claims.
The reply understates how readily fictional narratives can incorporate accurate people, places, and researched settings.
The move attacks a central external-attestation bridge at the textual and source-dependence levels.
Calling wholesale inauthenticity obvious overstates a position that the move itself says requires numerous disputed reasons.
The ordinary scarcity of records for obscure ancient people appropriately warrants the limited concession.
Choosing the most probable explanation is coherent, though this decision rule does not select an explanation itself.
The methodological claim is sensible but is asserted without applying explicit comparative probabilities here.
The reply accepts evidentiary defects and answers Carrier’s concession by restating the affirmative inferential standard.
The probability standard properly frames both sides' motion-level evidentiary burdens.
Certainty, possibility, and probability are distinctly and clearly contrasted.
Evans concedes bogus and interpolated evidence, but his high final confidence exceeds the comparison shown in this move.
Shared non-Markan material can imply another tradition, but early dating and historicity remain further steps.
The shared Matthew-Luke material is specific support, though independence and dating are incompletely defended.
The move directly answers the claim that Q contributes no meaningful early tradition.
Independent early teaching would materially support gospel roots, but does not alone establish factual content.
The no-Q alternative and inference to independent tradition are stated in understandable terms.
Evans acknowledges Goodacre’s intelligence and minority view, yet leans too heavily on majority acceptance.
The independent-tradition inference is clear, but its identification with an early historical source remains insufficiently secured.
Underdetermined dating and genre coherently block using hypothetical Q as early historical corroboration.
The lack of a surviving document supports caution, though the strongest internal dating arguments are not examined.
The move directly answers both the early-date and historical-content inferences made for Q.
It materially limits a proposed independent early source without demanding that Carrier prove a contrary date.
Existence, date, independence, and fictional status are separated with good analytical clarity.
Carrier conditionally grants Q's existence while limiting only the unsupported conclusions drawn from it.
A supper on a betrayal night naturally suggests earthly history, though alternative readings are not excluded.
The move directly answers the claim that Pauline markers remain wholly cosmic-compatible.
The meal, night, betrayal, and earthbound implication are clearly connected.
“This is not in outer space” expresses confidence beyond the textual location evidence presented.
The reply concerns celestial interpretation but only indirectly contacts Carrier’s first-century Pauline angel model.
Calling interpolation obvious and preservation efforts desperate overstates a contested textual inference and imputes motive.
The source explicitly supplies the contextual and terminological interpolation case, permitting high confidence in assessing its performed inference.
The Troy analogy clearly shows that verified setting does not logically verify a narrative protagonist.
Historically grounded fiction and archaeological Troy provide apt support for the limiting principle.
The move precisely answers the revised claim that verisimilitude functions as a historical screen.
It decisively limits what geographical accuracy can contribute to the historicity burden.
Setting verification and character verification are sharply distinguished through a concrete comparison.
The move grants the accurate setting and challenges only the excess inference drawn from it.
Granting theoretical precedent then appealing to specialist rejection is coherent but underexplains the rejection.
The positive concession is grounded in Carrier's examples, while the rebuttal relies chiefly on secondhand authority.
The move engages Carrier’s positive model rather than treating his position as merely an argument from silence.
It limits the analogy's application but does not independently show why the proposed parallels fail.
Evans explicitly calls this Carrier's best point and acknowledges his own secondhand reliance.
Lost correspondence and late composition coherently weaken arguments from unrecorded contemporary correction.
Chronology, survival estimates, and known historical-fiction practice support the reply, with some compressed claims.
The move answers both the absence-of-gainsaying claim and the archaeological-detail objection.
It materially limits two affirmative corroboration routes while avoiding a claim that loss proves fiction.
Eyewitness attrition, documentary blackout, and literary color are distinct despite the move's breadth.
The reply frames lost correction as an evidentiary limit and historical detail as compatible with fiction.
The chronology and documentary-loss thesis are explicit, but several dating, demographic, and literary-dependence claims remain contested.
The source states the dating and verbal-borrowing objection clearly, but the disputed Luke-Josephus relationship warrants medium confidence.
Evans fairly concedes visionary appearances but asserts earthbound historical presupposition beyond what physical burial alone shows.
The clarification preserves the con model but provides limited reason to prefer it over an earthly reading.
The cosmic physicality thesis is intelligible, but its scriptural parallels and reading of Pauline receipt remain substantially contestable.
A demonstrated mechanism would advance nonexistence, though much of this account remains speculative.
Carrier admits uncertainty about motives yet repeatedly describes gospel writers as producing fiction, duping readers, or lying.
Any incomplete affirmative links concerning Pauline contact, gospel corroboration, and external independence are already represented in the individual move dimensions.
Any incomplete comparative, celestial, source-dependence, or historicization inference is already captured in the corresponding move ratings.
